records.our_prose: A common approach is a lower-nitrogen complete fertilizer such as 5-10-10 worked into the bed before planting (Clemson cites about 30 pounds per 1,000 square feet, or a balanced scoop per hill), then a nitrogen side-dress about three to four weeks after planting as vines run, placed a few inches out from the plants and watered in, repeated lightly at flowering.

Melons should be side-dressed before the vines start to “run.” Side-dress with 34-0-0 at 1 pound per 100 feet of row or calcium nitrate (15.5-0-0) at 2 pounds per 100 feet of row.

records.our_prose: Watermelon is a moderate feeder that wants more phosphorus and potassium than nitrogen, since excess nitrogen drives leafy vine at the expense of fruit set and sugar. Work a lower-nitrogen complete fertilizer such as 5-10-10 into the bed before planting (Clemson suggests about 30 pounds per 1,000 square feet), then side-dress with a nitrogen source as the vines begin to run, and again lightly at flowering. Ease off nitrogen once fruit has set so the plant pours its energy into sizing and sweetening the melons rather than growing more vine. Pair feeding with even moisture, because the nutrients only help a plant that is not also drought-stressed.

records.our_prose: Try not to grow watermelon or its relatives (cucumbers, melons, squash) in the same spot more than once every 3 years, and wait longer, up to five years, if you have had wilt or anthracnose. Moving them around the garden is the best way to avoid a buildup of disease. Clean up old vines at the end of the season too.

records.source_context: Do not till bark or wood chip mulches into the soil close to plants, as they will tie up nitrogen as they decompose. Synthetic mulches should be removed and discarded at the end of the season or when they are no longer useful as mulches. Organic mulch materials can be turned into the soil with a spade or rototiller or placed in your compost pile.

records.our_prose: Pick a sunny spot with light, well-drained soil and mix in some compost before planting, but do not overdo rich, high-nitrogen material, or you get more vine than melon. Plant watermelon on low hills or mounds, which warm up and drain better. Give it lots of room: space hills about 4 to 8 feet apart for full-size types, since the vines can spread 8 to 12 feet (icebox and bush types need less). In cooler or shorter-summer areas, laying down black plastic mulch warms the soil and gives the plants an earlier, faster start. If your soil is heavy or stays wet, build the mounds up higher so water drains away from the roots and fruit.
